subject: maths
title: Year 5 Perimeter and Area
seo_title: Year 5 Perimeter and Area Worksheets: Free Maths with Answer Key (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Solve practical problems involving the perimeter and area of regular and irregular shapes using appropriate metric units
meta_desc: Free Year 5 perimeter and area worksheets for the Australian Curriculum (AC9M5M02): regular shapes, composite shapes with missing sides, length × width in cm² and m², estimating irregular areas on a grid and practical problems. 100 questions with an answer key, great for NAPLAN practice.
key_big: Perimeter: add every side. Area of a rectangle: length × width.
key_sub: Find missing sides first. Split composite shapes into rectangles and add their areas. Perimeter is in cm or m; area is in cm² or m².
body_html:
Perimeter and area

Perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape. It is a length: cm or m.

Area is the space inside a shape. It is measured in square units: cm² (square centimetres) or m² (square metres).

Perimeter of regular shapes

A regular shape has all sides the same length. Multiply the side length by the number of sides.

For a rectangle, add all 4 sides: 2 lengths and 2 widths.

Example

A rectangle is 9 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is its perimeter?

9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26. Or 2 × (9 + 4) = 26.

Answer: 26 cm

Perimeter of composite shapes

A composite rectilinear shape is made of rectangles joined together. Find the missing sides first, then add every side.

The short sides going across add up to the long side opposite. The same is true going up and down.

Area: count squares or use length × width

Count the 1 cm² squares inside the shape. For a rectangle, it is quicker to multiply.

Example

A rectangle has an area of 48 cm². It is 8 cm long. How wide is it?

Length × width = area, so width = 48 ÷ 8 = 6. Check: 8 × 6 = 48.

Answer: 6 cm

Area of composite shapes

Split the shape into rectangles. Find the area of each one, then add.

Estimating the area of irregular shapes

Curved shapes do not fit the squares exactly, so we estimate. Count each whole square. Count a square as 1 if half or more is covered. Leave out squares that are less than half covered.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Adding the sides to find the area (8 + 5 = 13)Area = length × width: 8 × 5 = 40 cm²
Multiplying to find the perimeterPerimeter: add all the sides
Using 4 sides for every shapeCount the sides: a triangle has 3, a hexagon has 6
Missing a hidden side in an L-shapeFind the missing sides first, then add every side
Counting every part square as a whole oneCount only squares that are half or more covered
Writing cm for an areaArea is in cm² or m². Perimeter is in cm or m

faq.q: What do Year 5 students learn about perimeter and area in the Australian Curriculum?
faq.a: They solve practical problems with the perimeter and area of regular and irregular shapes, using cm, m, cm² and m² (AC9M5M02). This includes composite rectangle shapes and estimating the area of curved shapes on a grid.

faq.q: What is the difference between perimeter and area?
faq.a: Perimeter is the distance around the outside of a shape, measured in cm or m. Area is the space inside, measured in square units such as cm² or m².

faq.q: How do you find the area of an irregular shape in Year 5?
faq.a: Split a shape with straight sides into rectangles and add their areas. For a curved shape, put it on a 1 cm grid and count the whole squares and the squares that are half or more covered.

faq.q: Are perimeter and area on the Year 5 NAPLAN numeracy test?
faq.a: NAPLAN numeracy is based on the Australian Curriculum, so Year 5 students can meet perimeter and area questions. Practising missing sides, length × width and word problems helps them prepare.

sets.title: Area: count squares or use length × width

items.q: A rectangle has an area of 90 m². It is 15 m long. How wide is it?
items.e: Length × width = area, so width = area ÷ length: 90 ÷ 15 = 6 m. Check: 15 × 6 = 90 m².

items.q: What is the area of this rectangle?
items.e: Area of a rectangle = length × width: 8 × 5 = 40 cm². 26 cm would be the perimeter.

items.q: Each square is 1 cm². What is the area of the shaded shape?
items.e: Count the whole squares inside the shape: 29. Or: 7 × 5 = 35 for the whole rectangle, take away the empty corner 3 × 2 = 6: 35 − 6 = 29 cm².

items.e: All the sides of a square are the same, so length and width are both 15 cm: 15 × 15 = 225 cm².

items.e: Count every whole square, and count a square as 1 if half or more of it is covered. Leave out squares that are less than half covered. The parts you count and leave out roughly balance.

sets.title: Practical problems: fences, carpet and gardens

items.q: A rectangular vegetable garden bed has timber edging all the way around. The edging is 34 m long. The bed is 11 m long. How wide is it?
items.e: The two long sides make 2 × 11 = 22 m. 34 − 22 = 12 m for the two short sides, so each is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 m.

items.q: A front lawn is 9 m long and 6 m wide. New turf costs $12 per square metre. How much does turf for the whole lawn cost?
The reading corner in a classroom is 4 m long and 3 m wide. It will be covered with carpet tiles. Four tiles cover 1 m². How many tiles are needed?
items.e: Area: 4 × 3 = 12 m². Each square metre needs 4 tiles: 12 × 4 = 48 tiles.

items.q: A bedroom wall is 5 m long and 3 m high. It has a door about 1 m wide and 2 m high. What area of wall needs painting?
items.e: Wall: 5 × 3 = 15 m². Door: 1 × 2 = 2 m². Take away the door: 15 − 2 = 13 m².

items.q: Ava’s backyard is 8 m by 6 m. Leo’s backyard is 7 m by 7 m. Which backyard has the larger area, and by how much?
items.e: Ava: 8 × 6 = 48 m². Leo: 7 × 7 = 49 m². 49 − 48 = 1 m². The perimeters are both 28 m, but the areas are different.

items.q: A rectangular paddock is 25 m long and 16 m wide. A fence goes all the way around, except for a gate 3 m wide. How much fence is needed?
items.e: Perimeter: 25 + 16 + 25 + 16 = 82 m. No fence across the gate: 82 − 3 = 79 m.

items.q: Mei is building a raised garden bed 3 m long and 2 m wide. What area of soil can she plant in?
items.e: Planting space is area: 3 × 2 = 6 m². (3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 10 m is the edge of the bed.)

items.q: Chloe is making a chook pen with an area of 36 m². It could be 9 m by 4 m or 6 m by 6 m. Which pen needs less wire fencing?
items.e: Both have an area of 36 m². Fence: 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26 m and 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24 m. The square needs less fence.

items.q: A backyard is 15 m long and 10 m wide. A swimming pool 8 m by 4 m is in the backyard. The rest is lawn. What area of lawn is there?
items.e: Backyard: 15 × 10 = 150 m². Pool: 8 × 4 = 32 m². Lawn: 150 − 32 = 118 m².

items.q: A school office floor is 6 m by 5 m. Each box of carpet tiles covers 4 m². How many boxes are needed to cover the floor?
items.e: Area: 6 × 5 = 30 m². 30 ÷ 4 = 7 remainder 2. 7 boxes cover only 28 m², so 8 boxes are needed.

items.q: This is the plan of an L-shaped family room. What area of carpet covers the whole floor?
items.e: Split into two rectangles: 6 × 2 = 12 and 10 × 3 = 30. Total: 12 + 30 = 42 m².
Whole squares: 7. Squares half or more covered: 6. Estimate: 7 + 6 = 13 m².

items.q: A square playground has a perimeter of 64 m. What is its area?
items.e: Each side: 64 ÷ 4 = 16 m. Area: 16 × 16 = 256 m².

items.q: Lachlan’s family is putting a new fence around their rectangular backyard. It is 18 m long and 12 m wide. How many metres of fence do they need?
items.e: The fence goes along all 4 sides: 18 + 12 + 18 + 12 = 60 m.

items.q: A rectangular poster for the school athletics carnival has an area of 600 cm². It is 30 cm wide. How tall is it?
items.e: Area = width × height, so height = 600 ÷ 30 = 20 cm. Check: 30 × 20 = 600 cm².

items.q: A basketball court is 28 m long and 15 m wide. What is its area?
A patio is 6 m long and 4 m wide. Each pallet of pavers covers 5 m². How many pallets are needed?
items.e: Area: 6 × 4 = 24 m². 24 ÷ 5 = 4 remainder 4. 4 pallets cover only 20 m², so 5 pallets are needed.

items.q: Mia has 20 m of edging to make a rectangular vegetable patch. Which patch has the largest area?
items.e: All four use 20 m of edging. Areas: 9 × 1 = 9 m², 8 × 2 = 16 m², 7 × 3 = 21 m², 5 × 5 = 25 m². The square has the largest area.

items.q: A classroom pinboard is 120 cm long and 90 cm wide. What is its area?
items.e: Length × width: 120 × 90 = 10 800 cm². Tip: 12 × 9 = 108, then × 100.

items.q: A cricket pitch is about 20 m long and 3 m wide. Estimate its area.
items.e: Area = length × width: 20 × 3 = 60 m². 46 m is the distance around it.
